overview: This file consists of a cross-reference sheet and a two-page consular despatch from Tokyo concerning semi-anthracite coal in northern Sakhalin. Consul General Arthur Garrels reports that no semi-anthracite was mined in southern, Japanese-controlled Sakhalin, then supplies analyses and production figures for the Due, Regatoi, and Meashi mines in Soviet northern Sakhalin. The despatch distinguishes Japanese-operated and Soviet-operated mines, notes the use of Regatoi coal as bunker fuel at Vladivostok and elsewhere in Russia, and records that information about northern Sakhalin’s port-loading facilities was unavailable.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Garrels despatch no. 131
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to another decimal-file location for Garrels’s despatch on semi-anthracite coal in Sakhalin.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers the reader to file 142.15/4189 for despatch no. 131 from Tokyo. It identifies Arthur Garrels and summarizes the despatch’s finding that no semi-anthracite coal was mined in southern, Japanese-controlled Sakhalin. The printed date appears in the OCR as February 10, 1901, but the surrounding file and the despatch itself establish the intended year as 1931.

subfiles.title: Analysis and production of semi-anthracite coal in northern Sakhalin
subfiles.about: Garrels provides coal analyses, production statistics, ownership information, and limited shipping information for mines in northern Sakhalin.
subfiles.summary: Responding to a Department of State memorandum and a request originating with the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Garrels reports that semi-anthracite was not mined in southern, Japanese Sakhalin. He gives the composition and annual output of the Japanese-operated Due Mine and the Soviet-operated Regatoi and Meashi mines in northern Sakhalin. Regatoi production was estimated at 50,000–60,000 long tons annually and was used as bunker coal at Vladivostok and elsewhere in Russia, while Meashi production was insignificant. Garrels could obtain no information about northern Sakhalin’s port-loading facilities.

interest: The file offers compact quantitative evidence about the composition and output of northern Sakhalin coal at the beginning of the 1930s, including moisture, volatile matter, ash, and fixed-carbon percentages. It is especially useful for comparing a Japanese-operated concession with Soviet government mines and for tracing the commercial intelligence exchanged among American diplomatic posts, the Department of State, and the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. The contrast between detailed mine statistics and the admitted lack of information on port-loading facilities also illustrates the practical limits of U.S. economic reporting in Soviet northern Sakhalin.
